newsitem.title: FRANCE: Borotra defends Renault plant closure.
newsitem.headline: Borotra defends Renault plant closure.

text.p: French Industry Minister Franck Borotra said on Tuesday that a decision by Renault SA to close a factory in Belgium and cut jobs was needed to reduce costs and return the car operations to equilibrium in 1997 and 1998.
He told parliament during question time that he urged the company to consult with its social partners and follow the law to the letter.
"In 1995, the car operations of Renault made a loss of 1.7 billion francs ($295 million). In 1996, the car market increased strongly in our country -- more than 10 percent growth," he said.

"Despite this favourable car market situation, Renault lost 2.6 points in market share in France and I read in newspapers that the operating loss of the car operations will be about three billion francs," he added.

"1997 will be an unfavourable year for the car sector because we are expecting a fall of 10 to 12 percent in car sales in the French market," he said. "At the end of February, sales were down 21 percent compared to February 1996.

"In consequence competition will be fiercer because the market is smaller. And the competition will be almost exclusively on price. Therefore (car) companies have to be able to be competitive to face this competition," he said.

"If the company does not take measures to cut its costs and thus engage in the necessary restructuring, it will neither in 1997 nor in 1998 be able to return to equilibrium and on January 1, 2000, when we have to open the market to full world competition and in particular Asian countries, it will be too late...," Borotra said.
"Today there is an unavoidable economic objective for Renault -- the necessity to cut its sales prices, to reduce costs and create conditions of competition and safeguard the future.

"That cannot happen except as part of an industrial strategy and it is up to the management of Renault to select this strategy and to put it in place, while respecting the law and, clearly, social interests and the interests of the regions where the plants are based," he said.

"What I wish is that dialogue will be put in place with the social partners, that contact be maintained with the Belgian authorities but at the same time that the company realises that to face the competition in the year 2000, the future of this great company is being decided today," Borotra said.
"Companies that are not able to face competition are in the end companies that will disappear," he added.
Renault, 46 percent owned by the French government since a two stage privatisation in 1994 and 1996, on Thursday announced the closure in June of its Vilvoorde plant in Belgium.
This will cut 3,100 direct jobs and another 1,100 at supplying companies.
On Tuesday, the company informed unions of plans to shed another 2,764 jobs in France in 1997.
